title: Renewables in Electricity Markets
text:
At the Technical University of Denmark, I developed and taught for many years an M.Sc. course on Renewables in Electricity Markets. All the course material is shared here for anyone who wants to learn about the topic. It covers the basics of electricity markets (day-ahead and balancing markets, ancillary services), the impact of renewables on markets, how renewable energy producers participate in electricity markets, and renewable energy analytics, mainly forecasting.
The course is built from ten modules of video lectures with slides. Six exercise sessions let you apply the ideas, and interviews with industry guests and former students show why it matters in practice.

title: Renewables in Electricity Markets
text:
Why renewables in electricity markets?
The topic sits where three of the major trends in electric energy systems over the last 10 to 20 years meet: the large-scale deployment of renewable energy generation, the deregulation of the electric power sector, and digitization. title: Probabilistic forecasting
text:
A forecast is only as useful as the decisions it supports. For most decisions in energy, from trading to grid operation, that means knowing not only the most likely outcome but how uncertain it is.
When I started working on wind power forecasting in the early 2000s, forecasts were almost always single values. My work since then has helped make probabilistic forecasts the norm in energy: forecasts given as full predictive distributions, quantiles, intervals or scenarios. That has meant developing the methods to produce them, the tools to check that they can be trusted, and showing how decision-makers can use them.

title: Probabilistic forecasting
text:
From prediction intervals to scenarios
Many decisions depend on how a quantity evolves over time, for instance how much energy to store, or how much flexibility to keep for the next hours. Prediction intervals for each hour taken separately are then not enough: two very different futures can share exactly the same intervals. Scenarios fill that gap by describing whole trajectories, with realistic dependence from one hour to the next.

  
    
  
  
    Temporal dependence  
    New scenarios
  
  The shaded bands are the 50% and 80% prediction intervals, and the dashed line the median. Hour by hour, the scenarios are consistent with these intervals, so about one in five falls outside the 80% band at any given time. With low dependence they jump around implausibly from hour to hour; with high dependence they behave like real wind power trajectories. The approach follows our 2009 paper on generating scenarios from probabilistic forecasts.

title: Probabilistic forecasting
text:
Main contributions
Methods. Nonparametric and parametric approaches to probabilistic forecasting of wind, solar, wave, load and market quantities, including generalised logit-Normal distributions that respect the bounds of wind power generation, regime-switching models for offshore wind fluctuations, and conditional prediction intervals.
Verification. A framework for assessing probabilistic forecasts, based on reliability, sharpness and skill, that is now widely used to evaluate energy forecasts, along with work on reliability diagrams that accounts for serial correlation.
Space, time and dependence. Scenario generation from probabilistic forecasts, spatio-temporal models that exploit information from geographically dispersed sites, and sparse and online vector autoregressive models for high-dimensional forecasting.
Learning from distributed data. Distributed, online and privacy-preserving learning, so that wind and solar farms can improve their forecasts together without sharing raw data, and value-oriented forecast reconciliation for decision-making.
Building the field. Co-organising the Global Energy Forecasting Competitions (GEFCom2012 and GEFCom2014), which set benchmarks for the community, and serving as Editor-in-Chief of the International Journal of Forecasting from 2019 to 2026.

title: Data and analytics markets
text:
Better forecasts often depend on data held by others: neighbouring wind farms, weather providers, other market participants. Data and analytics markets give them a reason to share, by paying each for what their data is actually worth.
Collaborative forecasting can improve accuracy a great deal, but data owners rarely share for free, and they may worry about privacy. My recent work develops markets that allocate the value created by data, forecasts and models fairly among those who contribute them, starting from privacy-preserving collaborative learning and leading to regression markets, wagering mechanisms for forecasts, and analytics markets that are robust to strategic behaviour such as replicating data.

title: Data and analytics markets
text:
A regression market
In a regression market, a forecaster states how much an improvement in forecast quality is worth to them. Data sellers offer their data, a model is fitted with it, and each seller is paid according to their marginal contribution to the improvement, measured with Shapley values from cooperative game theory. Useful data earns money, redundant data earns less, and irrelevant data earns nothing.

title: Energy markets
text:
Electricity markets were designed for controllable power plants. With large shares of wind and solar power, both how producers trade and how markets are organised need to account for uncertainty.
My work on energy markets follows two threads. The first is how renewable energy producers and other participants should trade, using probabilistic forecasts and decision-making under uncertainty. The second is how markets themselves should be designed and cleared, from stochastic market-clearing and coordination between electricity, gas and heat markets, to peer-to-peer and community-based markets.

title: Energy markets
section: Trading wind energy with probabilistic forecasts
text:
Trading wind energy with probabilistic forecasts
A wind farm must commit to its production a day ahead, before knowing the weather. Any deviation is settled in the balancing market, usually at a penalty. If falling short is penalised more than producing too much, the best offer is below the expected production, and the other way round. With a probabilistic forecast, the optimal offer is a specific quantile of the predictive distribution, set by the ratio of the two penalties. This is the classic newsvendor problem, and the insight behind our 2007 paper on trading wind generation.

  Day-ahead price set at €50/MWh. The predictive distribution is bounded by zero and the 100 MW capacity of the wind farm. Making the penalties asymmetric, or the forecast more uncertain, moves the optimal offer away from the point forecast and increases what is gained by using the full distribution.

title: Energy markets
text:
Main contributions
Trading strategies. Offering strategies for renewable producers based on probabilistic forecasts, extended to price-maker producers, wind-storage systems, energy and reserve markets, online decision-making and distributionally robust strategies.
Market design and clearing. Stochastic market-clearing that dispatches renewables while accounting for their uncertainty, with attention to revenue adequacy and cost recovery, as well as new market products and conic market formulations.
Coordination between markets. Integrated and coordinated markets for electricity, natural gas and heat, and coordination across regions and between transmission and distribution levels.
Consumer-centric markets. Peer-to-peer and community-based electricity markets, including the design of energy collectives, product differentiation, and fair allocation of grid costs.

title: My take on future electricity markets
text:
Should the organisation, design and functioning of electricity markets be taken for granted? Definitely not.
After decades of liberalised electricity markets in places like the U.K., Scandinavia and Chile, it is tempting to think we found the right, future-proof model. My view is that we have not. Renewable generation, decentralisation, electrification and digitalisation are changing power systems so fundamentally that markets have to be redesigned to be fit for purpose. That means seeing them as mechanisms for organising and operating a socio-techno-economic system, not only as a way to exchange a commodity. Some basics are not negotiable, such as the laws of physics and marginal pricing of energy, but many other aspects can, and should, be rethought.

title: My take on future electricity markets
section: What markets are for: three perspectives
text:
What markets are for: three perspectives
Economic. Markets allocate resources, reveal prices for payments and revenues, and give signals for investment, while keeping desirable properties such as participants not entering at a loss, honest participation and budget balance.
Engineering. Markets help operate the largest and most complex engineering system ever built. The hard question is where to draw the line between what can and should be handled through markets, and what cannot.
Environmental, social and governance. Markets should support decarbonisation, but they also reflect how we want to produce, share and consume energy, with growing attention to fairness, energy poverty, community ownership and consumers’ preferences about where their electricity comes from.

title: My take on future electricity markets
section: Seeing it in a simple market
text:
Seeing it in a simple market
The illustration below clears a stylised day-ahead market for every hour of a day. Increase the share of wind and solar power, and watch what happens to prices and to what renewable producers earn. Then let part of the demand follow supply.

  
    
  
  
    
  
  
    Wind and solar capacity   GW

  Stylised illustration, not a model of any real market. Supply: wind and solar at zero marginal cost, then nuclear, coal, gas and peaking plants. Demand is mostly inflexible, with a small price-responsive part. Wind and solar are assumed to need about €45/MWh on average to recover their investment.

With little renewable generation, prices are set by fossil plants and renewables earn well. As their share grows, more and more hours clear at a price close to zero, so wind and solar earn less precisely when there is more of them, and marginal pricing alone no longer pays back the investment. Letting flexible demand follow supply, instead of supply following demand, absorbs surplus renewable energy and, at moderate shares of renewables, lifts what they earn. With very large surpluses, though, there is not enough demand to move, and prices stay near zero. That is one reason why a growing part of the remuneration of assets is likely to shift to auctions and capacity mechanisms.

title: My take on future electricity markets
section: Expected features of future electricity markets
text:
Expected features of future electricity markets
Variability, uncertainty and flexibility. Markets designed for controllable plants treat offers as deterministic. With weather-driven generation and new consumption such as heat pumps and electric vehicles, they should move towards stochastic electricity markets, allowing probabilistic offers, new products such as policy-based reserves and price-region bids, and pricing that reflects firmness of supply and flexibility of demand.
Distributed and coordinated. Assets are increasingly small and distributed, so markets should let consumers and prosumers take part, through lower minimum bid sizes, aggregators, and community-based and peer-to-peer markets, possibly leading wholesale and retail markets to converge. Electricity, gas and heat markets also need better coordination, or joint markets, to integrate renewables.
Data-driven and fair. Data and analytics already underpin new market designs. As decentralisation grows, AI-based approaches may help clear markets that would otherwise be computationally out of reach, and make room for fairness objectives alongside social welfare. With renewable energy close to free at the margin, data may even become more valuable than energy itself, which calls for data-sharing platforms that preserve privacy.
A changing role for wholesale markets. Renewable-based systems shift costs from operation to investment. A growing part of the remuneration of assets is then likely to move to auctions and capacity mechanisms, while new, often more cooperative business models emerge on the retail side, from co-investing in wind farms to sharing surplus solar power.

title: International Journal of Forecasting
text:
The International Journal of Forecasting (IJF) is the leading journal in its field. It is the official publication of the International Institute of Forecasters (IIF) and shares its aims and scope: to unify the field and bridge the gap between theory and practice, making forecasting useful and relevant for decision and policy makers. The journal places strong emphasis on empirical studies, evaluation, implementation research and ways of improving forecasting practice, and is open to many points of view. Reviewing is double-blind.
I wrote an editorial in early 2020 when I became Editor-in-Chief.

title: International Journal of Forecasting
text:
Topics covered
Economic and econometric forecasting, marketing, new products, finance, production, technology, business, government and the military, demographics, energy, climate, crime, seasonal adjustment, time series, legal and political aspects, implementation, judgmental and psychological aspects, the impact of forecast uncertainty on decision making, organizational aspects, sport, machine learning, forecasting methodology, elections, and big data.
The journal publishes research papers, research notes, discussion articles, book reviews, editorials and letters. Data and code associated with published articles are provided as online supplements on ScienceDirect.

title: International Journal of Forecasting

The IJF welcomes submissions relevant to the science and practice of forecasting: methodological and applied papers, new datasets and forecasting competitions, short communications, book reviews and interviews.

Online supplements. For empirical studies, the description of the method and data should allow replication. Please submit code and data to be published as an online supplement. Appendices with additional results can be supplements too.
